title: Simplify Path
prompt:
Given an absolute path for a Unix-style file system, which begins with `/`, transform it into its simplified canonical path.

In a Unix-style file system, a single period `.` refers to the current directory, a double period `..` refers to the parent directory, and multiple consecutive slashes are treated as a single slash. The canonical path should have exactly one slash between directory names, must not end with a trailing slash unless it's the root, and must use only single periods to represent single-level directories where actually needed (i.e. `.` and `..` are resolved away, not kept literally).
constraints: path consists of English letters, digits, '.', '/', or '_'
path is a valid absolute Unix path
hints: Splitting the path on '/' gives you a sequence of components you can process one at a time, keeping track of the current directory stack.
A stack of directory names naturally models '..' (pop the last directory) and ignores empty segments / '.' (do nothing).
After processing every component, join whatever remains on the stack with '/' and prefix with a leading '/' — if the stack is empty, the canonical path is just '/'.

solution.approach: Split the path on '/' to get individual components (this naturally collapses consecutive slashes into empty strings that can be skipped). Walk the components with a stack representing the current directory path: skip empty strings and '.', pop the stack on '..' (if non-empty, since you can't go above root), and push any other real directory name. Finally join the stack with '/' and prepend a leading '/' to form the canonical path.
